newsitem.title: USA: Dayton Hudson could sell more stores.
newsitem.headline: Dayton Hudson could sell more stores.

text.p: Dayton Hudson Corp., which recently agreed to sell four department stores in Texas, said Tuesday it would consider shedding more non-core stores if the price was right.
Dayton Hudson, the nation's fourth-largest retailer, announced plans in August to sell four Marshall Field's stores in Texas -- one to Federated Department Stores Inc. and three to Saks Holdings Inc.

Chief Financial Officer Douglas Scovanner said the retailer unloaded the stores because they were outside the Upper Midwest base of its department store division. The retailer is the parent of Marshall Field's, Dayton's and Hudson's department stores.
Minneapolis-based Dayton Hudson could consider shedding other stores located outside its core markets.
"Yes, we would certainly consider disposition of non-strategic stores if we found willing buyers ready to pay enough to make it worth our while to sell," Scovanner said in an interview.
In addition to the department store division, Dayton Hudson owns discounter Target and California-based Mervyn's.

Mervyn's, the company's troubled chain of 300 moderately priced department stores, has stores in 16 states. Its key markets include California, where it operates about 128 stores, and Texas, home of about 45 Mervyn's outlets.
But the farther away from California Mervyn's gets, the lower its market share becomes, with certain exceptions such as Texas.
In Florida and Georgia, Mervyn's customer base is lower than in California, Scovanner said. He declined to say whether the company has considered getting rid of those stores.
"We clearly have talked to analysts about the fact that our market shares are lower in Florida and Georgia at Mervyn's than in California," he said. "That's a well-known fact."
Mervyn's has been a drag on Dayton Hudson's results for several years. The chain's operating profit dropped by more than half to $100 million in 1995 from $206 million in 1994.

This year, Dayton Hudson unleashed a company cost-cutting programme that calls for a $100 million expense reduction over two years at the chain. Mervyn's also has held fewer clearance sales, beefed up merchandise selection and boosted its gross margin. Its operating profit climbed to $54 million in the second quarter from $3 million last year, but sales fell.
Sales remain soft this quarter.

Mervyn's same-store sales, or sales among stores open a year, were at the low end of the company's expectations for a decline in the low-to-mid single digits in percentage terms during September, Scovanner said.
But even though its sales have been poor, Mervyn's already has cleared minimal benchmarks for profit gains set by Dayton Hudson earlier this year.
"Mervyn's financial performance has fully tracked our internal plan," he added.
With Mervyn's earnings growth coming largely from cost cutting this year, analysts said the company soon will have to put sales back on track in order to keep profits rising.
Scovanner said Mervyn's same-store sales should increase next year. But if they don't, Dayton Hudson could face pressure from investors to get rid of the unit, analysts said.
"The cost-cutting at Mervyn's can only go so far," said Patrick McCormack of Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

Analysts said if Dayton Hudson were to decide to divest Mervyn's, it probably would not choose to sell it off piecemeal. Instead, the company would wait until Mervyn's results improved before selling off the whole chain to an outsider or spinning it off to shareholders, they said.
"I don't think the issues at Mervyn's can be solved by selling off particular markets," said Dean Ramos of Dain Bosworth Inc.
